lines.text: The family is the most fundamental social unit in every culture. A typical nuclear family consists of parents — a mother and father — and their children: sons and daughters. Siblings, whether brothers or sisters, grow up together and share formative experiences. In many households, the parents are a married couple — a husband and wife — though modern families come in many forms, including single-parent families. Family roles have evolved significantly. Traditionally, the father was the breadwinner while the mother was the homemaker, but today both parents often share professional and domestic responsibilities equally. Children transition from being infants cared for entirely by their parents to becoming independent adults who eventually start their own families. Family bonds are reinforced through daily routines — shared meals, homework help, bedtime stories — and through celebrations like birthdays, holidays, and family reunions. Communication within a family shapes children's development: supportive parents raise confident children, while a nurturing home environment builds emotional security. Understanding family vocabulary is essential because family is one of the first and most frequent topics in any language.

lines.text: In English-speaking countries, the 'nuclear family' (parents + children) is the standard unit discussed, unlike many cultures where the extended family living together is the norm. However, this is changing with multigenerational households becoming more common.

lines.text: English speakers typically call parents 'Mum/Mom' and 'Dad'. In formal contexts or when speaking about them, 'my mother' and 'my father' are used. Children rarely use first names for parents — this is considered disrespectful in most English-speaking families.

lines.text: Terms like 'stepmother', 'stepfather', 'stepsister', 'half-brother' are common in English as blended families are widespread. These terms carry no negative connotation in modern usage — they simply describe family structure after remarriage.

lines.text: Being an 'only child' (having no siblings) is common and carries no stigma in English-speaking cultures. The phrase 'only child syndrome' exists but is considered outdated. Many people proudly identify as an only child.

lines.text: Modern English increasingly uses gender-neutral terms: 'parent' instead of 'mother/father', 'sibling' instead of 'brother/sister', 'spouse' or 'partner' instead of 'husband/wife'. These are especially common in formal and inclusive contexts.
